1.title: Incident Response
1.text: Welcome to Module fifteen: Incident Response. It covers the exam area five. Security Operations and Incident Response. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. five point three Understand Incident Response (I R): Data handling policy implementing Incident Response Plan (I R P). Incident Response (I R) exercises (for example testing, tabletop). Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: five. Security Operations and Incident Response (seventeen point three percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: Events, incidents and the plan
1.text: Events, incidents and the plan. Event. Any observable occurrence in a system. Incident. An event that actually or potentially harms confidentiality, integrity or availability, or breaks policy. Breach. An incident in which protected data is disclosed to unauthorized people. An incident response plan (I R P) is the documented plan for how the organization detects, handles and learns from incidents. It lists roles, severity levels, steps, contacts and communication rules. An incident response team has members from security, I T, legal, communications, H R and management. Exam tip: The plan is written before the incident. During an incident follow the plan; do not improvise.

1.title: The incident response phases
1.text: The incident response phases. The figure shows this: The incident response life cycle from preparation to lessons learned.

1.title: The incident response phases, continued
1.text: The incident response phases. one Preparation. Plan, team, tools, training, contacts, tested playbooks. two Detection and analysis. Spot the incident (alerts, reports), confirm it, rate its severity, scope it. three Containment. Limit the damage: isolate hosts, disable accounts, block addresses. four Eradication. Remove the cause: delete malware, close the vulnerability, patch. five Recovery. Restore systems from clean backups, monitor for return. six Post-incident activity. Lessons learned: review what happened, update the plan and controls. Phases three to five are grouped as containment, eradication and recovery in the nist guide. Containment comes before eradication: stop the spread first, then clean. Exam tip: Prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Contain first: do not delete evidence or rebuild before you understand and limit the attack.

1.title: Data handling in the plan
1.text: Data handling in the plan. A data handling policy tells responders how to treat information during an incident. Classification applies. Incident data (logs, copies of systems) is handled by its sensitivity. Need to know. Share details only with those who must know. Legal and regulatory notice. Laws may require telling regulators or customers within a deadline; legal counsel decides. Communication. One spokesperson; do not discuss on public channels.

1.title: Data handling in the plan, continued
1.text: Data handling in the plan. Evidence handling. Chain of custody. A record of who held the evidence and when, so it stays trustworthy. Order of volatility. Collect the most short-lived data first: memory, then running processes and network state, then disk, then logs and backups. Forensic copy and hash. Work on a copy; a hash proves the copy matches the original. Exam tip: Chain of custody keeps evidence admissible. Memory is collected before disk because it disappears when the power is off.

1.title: Exercises and testing
1.text: Exercises and testing. A plan that is never tested fails when needed. Read-through or checklist. What happens: Team reviews the plan. Impact: None. Tabletop. What happens: Team discusses a scenario around a table. Impact: None on systems. Walkthrough. What happens: Team steps through actual procedures. Impact: Low. Simulation. What happens: Acts out a scenario, possibly with test systems. Impact: Low. Full exercise. What happens: Real actions against live or realistic systems. Impact: Higher. After each exercise, record findings and update the plan. Automation and A I: playbooks and automated tools handle routine, repeatable steps such as blocking a known bad address; a person decides about serious or unusual incidents.

1.title: Related plans
1.text: Related plans. I R P. Handles the security incident. Disaster recovery plan. Restores I T if the incident destroys systems. Business continuity plan. Keeps the business running while it is handled.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A malware infection is confirmed on a server. What should the team do first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Contain the incident by isolating the server. Containment limits the damage and comes before eradication and recovery.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Which phase includes removing malware and closing the vulnerability that allowed the attack? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Eradication. Eradication removes the cause of the incident.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. After an incident, the team meets to review what happened and improve the plan. Which phase is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Post-incident activity, which captures lessons learned. The review and plan update belong to post-incident activity.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which data should a responder collect first from a running compromised computer? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Memory contents, which are lost at power off. The order of volatility says to collect memory first because it disappears when power is lost.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A team talks through a ransomware scenario around a table without touching any system. What is this exercise? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A tabletop exercise that is a discussion. A discussion-based scenario exercise is a tabletop exercise.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A record shows who held a disk image, when and where it was stored. What does this record support? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Chain of custody of the evidence. A record of who held evidence and when is the chain of custody.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What are the phases of incident response? Answer: Preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, post-incident activity. Question two. What does an I R P list? Answer: Roles, severity levels, steps, contacts and communication rules. Question three. What is chain of custody? Answer: A record of who held the evidence and when.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which data is collected first by the order of volatility? Answer: Memory. Question five. Does a tabletop exercise touch real systems? Answer: No, it is a discussion. Question six. Who decides about legal notification of a breach? Answer: Legal counsel with management.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Definitions: event, incident (harm or threat), breach (data disclosed). Phases: prepare, detect and analyze, contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Data handling: classification, need to know, legal notice, one spokesperson. Evidence: chain of custody, order of volatility, hashed copy. Exercises: read-through, tabletop, walkthrough, simulation, full.
